en: *Chan Zong Zhi Zhang* (Pointing at the Palm of the Hand:
The Chan School), composed by the junior monk Xinghai. Part One.
I have heard that for those dwelling in the mundane world, the principle of the Middle Way is paramount; for those who have transcended the dust of the world, the power of Prajñā is essential.

If one dwells in the mundane world while deviating from the Middle Way, every undertaking will lose its standard. If one has transcended the dust of the world but fails to attain Prajñā, one will inevitably fall into the path of demons.
Now, the general purport of the Buddha-dharma is simply to clarify the Middle Way, the primary ultimate truth, which is the wondrous emptiness of true reality.
Regarding principle: if one does not attain the fundamental great wisdom of *prajñā*, one cannot clearly comprehend the wondrous principle of ultimate truth, which is true emptiness.
What is this Middle Way of ultimate truth, the wondrous principle of true emptiness? It is said to be neither empty nor existent;
neither annihilated nor eternal; without gain and without loss; without ordinary beings and without sages; without birth-and-death and without nirvāṇa.
In brief, there are no phenomena whatsoever, whether mundane or supramundane; even the path of language is severed, and the sphere of mental activity is extinguished.
Thus, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "There is only verbal expression; there is no real meaning at all. The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says:
"Whatever has marks is entirely false and illusory. The *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "Even if there were a single dharma that surpassed nirvāṇa..."
"Bhā" means that I also say it is like an illusion and like a transformation (and so forth). Why is this so? Because it is solely the single True Mind.
For what reason? It is because all phenomena of the mundane and supramundane worlds—whether ordinary or sagely—do not transcend my own single True Mind.
Thus, in the *Sūtra of the Dharma-Door of the Pure Seal Asked by Bodhisattva Sāgaramati*, Chapter...

Seventh, Cloud: Furthermore, the Buddha told Śāriputra: "For example, it is like Jīvaka, the King of Physicians, who surveys the entire earth and sees that there is no grass or tree that is not medicine. A bodhisattva practicing the Prajñāpāramitā is also like this:
they observe all phenomena and see that there is nothing that is not bodhi. The commentary states: "Bodhi" is precisely the true mind. Since...
All phenomena (*dharma*) are *bodhi*. Thus, all phenomena are the true mind.
Since all phenomena are my own true mind, one does not perceive any phenomena at all. This is precisely the meaning of the saying:
"Once you recognize your own mind, there is not a single inch of earth. Since the myriad dharmas are all one's own true mind, how could the great earth not be the mind?
Yes. The great earth is oneself; it is entirely one’s own true mind. How could there be even a single inch of land to be obtained?
Not only is not a single inch of land obtainable, but not even a single atom can be obtained.
If even one-hundredth of an atom could be obtained, then the principle of "Mind-Only" would not be established. It is just like the great earth. One—
All phenomena are likewise so. Only in this way can it be called the supreme vehicle (*ekayāna*) of the wondrous principle of true emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

Therefore, the "clumsy deliverance" (*zhuòdù*) of the two vehicles analyzes phenomena to clarify emptiness; they fall into a biased emptiness and cannot take the myriad phenomena as their own essence.
In the teachings, they are disparaged as "withered sprouts and rotten seeds"—those who sever the lineage of the Buddha. If even the two vehicles are thus, how much more so for those below them?
This can now be understood. [The interlocutor] asks: "What has been explained above is that the myriad dharmas are the self-true mind;
thus, not even a hair’s breadth of a dharma exists apart from the mind. This principle is extremely clear and manifestly visible, leaving no room for doubt.
Yet you further state that it is 'neither empty nor existent' and so forth. What is the meaning of this? Please explain the reason. [The respondent] answers: "Empty" means non-existence.
Now, since it is called "one mind," how could it be empty and non-existent? Since it is solely one mind, how could it be existent?
Generally speaking, to be called "existent" requires two things to be in opposition so that existence can be established—namely, a subject that possesses and an object that is possessed.
Now, there is only the single true mind; in relation to what thing could it be called existent? Therefore, it is said to be neither empty nor existent. As for "not severed":
This refers to a certain class of people who do not awaken to the wondrous principle of their own mind’s true emptiness.

Upon hearing such statements as "there is no person and no self," "neither form nor emptiness," and "all marks whatsoever are entirely illusory," because they have not awakened to this truth, they falsely claim that the Dharmakāya is identical to non-existence or inert emptiness, thereby falling into the error of nihilism. Thus, it is stated in the *Zongjing lu*, fascicle 92.

It is said: "If it were neither form nor emptiness, and entirely devoid of discrimination, then those who have not seen their true nature would, upon reaching this state, fall completely into annihilation.
They would thus be identical to the non-Buddhist Kūṣmāṇḍas and others, whose own eyes are unopened; they mistake the obscure for the *amṛta-tattva* (the principle of primordial darkness).
Taking this silent, dark, and ignorant state as the ultimate, they further establish twenty-five principles (*tattva*) from this point on, remaining deluded regarding the Truth."
This is the true mind. It forms the seed of the non-Buddhist paths (tīrthika). Or there may be those in the Chan school who have not attained the essential meaning;

these are people of the Dharma-learned school who give rise to views of emptiness, for the most part brushing away both mind and objects to claim they are both empty. They cling to non-discrimination, taking their wild interpretations and ignorant blindness to be the ultimate Way. (And so forth.
Now, since this is called "one mind," how could it be the same as that void, stubborn emptiness of nihilistic annihilation? Therefore, it is said:
"Not discontinuous, not permanent" refers to those who have attachments, taking the illusory body of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) to be a true self.

They fall into the view of permanence (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*) and transmigrate through birth and death. Furthermore, various non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) cling to the idea that within the body of the five aggregates there exists a true, eternal self.
Because of this clinging, they do not attain liberation. Now, since there is only the single True Mind, how could two separate entities exist?

[Objection: "But does this not lead to the view of eternalism (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*)? For it is said that wherever there is grasping (*upādāna*), it must consist of two things to constitute grasping—namely, the grasper (*grāhaka*) and the grasped (*grāhya*).
Now, since there is only the single True Mind, grasping cannot be established; thus, one falls into the view of eternalism. [Response: Therefore, it is said to be "not eternal.
Regarding "there is nothing to be attained": since there is only the One Mind, how could there be anything to be attained? As for what is called "attainment," there must necessarily be two [factors].
Things must exist in mutual relation for an attainment to be possible; that is to say, there must be both an attainer and the object attained.

Now, since there is only the single true mind, how could there be external objects in opposition to it such that an attainment could be established? Therefore, it is said that there is "no gain and no loss."

Since it is called the sole true mind, manifesting in its full majesty, what could possibly be lost? Therefore, it is said that there is "no loss. Regarding the phrase "no ordinary beings" and so forth:

"ordinary" refers to the six realms of ordinary beings, and "sages" refers to the four classes of noble ones. "Birth and death" refers to mundane phenomena, and "nirvana" refers to supramundane phenomena.
Since all phenomena of the ten dharma-realms—both mundane and supramundane—are identical to one's own mind, how could there be any further birth and death?
Can any such phenomena be apprehended? Therefore, all things are non-existent. Regarding the phrase "the path of language is cut off and the sphere of mental activity is extinguished":
since all phenomena—mundane and supramundane, ordinary and sagely—are empty and non-existent, what further phenomenon could there be to take as a form or to express in words?
Since there is only the single true mind, how could there be a second phenomenon to serve as an object of that mind’s perception?
Indeed. The mind does not take itself as its own object, just as the eye cannot see itself, a finger cannot touch itself, and a blade cannot cut itself.

There must necessarily be a dharma that serves as the object of the mind; only then can the mind arise. Now, if there is only this single true mind and no other dharma to serve as the mind’s object, then this mind would have no object upon which to arise and would thus remain profoundly still and unmoving. Therefore, it is said: [The text continues with the verse].

The path of speech is cut off; the sphere of mental activity ceases. Furthermore, although the meaning of the "one mind" has been explained above, even so, no characteristic of mind can be apprehended.
This is based on conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), not ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), because within ultimate truth, the path of speech is cut off.
If one were to cling to the notion that a real, attainable true mind exists, this would constitute a false view and would not accord with correct principle. Question: Since...
Question: If it is the true mind, why is it also unattainable? Answer: By what means do you seek to attain it?
He replied: I seek to attain it by means of the mind. The Master said: If you seek to attain it by means of the mind, this is using the mind to grasp the mind;
does such a principle exist? Therefore, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva said: "I do not seek bodhi. Why? Because bodhi is myself, and I am bodhi. Furthermore, a sutra says:

It is said: "The harm caused by a wheel of swords that slaughters the people of Jambudvīpa is still minor compared to the fault of one who possesses the notion of attainment while preaching the Mahāyāna;

the latter's sin exceeds the former. Furthermore, the *Treatise on the Awakening of Faith* states: "That which is called 'not empty' refers to the manifestation of the essence of phenomena, for it is empty of falsehood.
This is the true mind, eternally constant and unchanging. Because it is fully endowed with pure dharmas, it is termed 'not empty. It also says:
There are no characteristics to be grasped, because it is a realm free from discursive thought, accessible only through realization and correspondence.
In the second chapter, a question is asked: "How can the wondrously luminous true mind be known? The answer is: "If one can realize emptiness without falling [into nihilism]..."

One eliminates the view of nihilism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*). Knowing that [the mind] exists without falling into the view of eternalism (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*) is precisely what is called the non-delusory true mind.

[The questioner] asks: "Please show me why this is so. [The teacher] answers: "A brief illustration may suffice for understanding. For example, the eye cannot see itself; yet this does not mean the eye does not exist.

Because the eye exists, one does not fall into the view of nihilism; because it does not see [itself], one does not fall into the extreme of eternalism. The eye serves as a metaphor for the True [Mind]."

The mind does not see itself; this is like being without delusion. Because the mind does not see itself, it is said to be empty, yet this does not mean that the self-substance of the mind is non-existent.
The true mind transcends all dependencies and may thus be called "true. Since the mind does not see itself, it may be considered free from delusion.
This principle is subtle and extremely difficult to exhaustively realize; without having accumulated vast roots of goodness and possessing keen intelligence and wisdom, one cannot penetrate it.
The guest said, "It is truly as you have stated.
As for the third article:
in the practice of Chan, it is vital to employ skillful means in the application of the mind. If one does not apply the mind skillfully, one will frequently incur faults and transgressions."

Consequently, one will encounter demonic obstacles, becoming deluded and losing one's mind. At the very least, one will mistake the false for the true and take the empty for the real, thereby wasting an entire lifetime and making it difficult to avoid the perverse result of evil karma arising from wholesome causes. How can one not be cautious?
For there are many types of misguided mental application, all of which are subsumed under two categories: first, attachment to existence; second, [attachment to emptiness].
These two types of views are both clung to by non-Buddhists and are not subsumed within the Buddha-dharma.
Nowadays, when people practice Chan meditation, although they know that the physical body is illusory, they nevertheless cling to the notion that the spiritual nature is real.
They claim that within the physical body there exists a luminous, awakened awareness, and they take this faculty of thought and discrimination to be the true self.
Some cling to the suppression of discursive thoughts, believing that when not a single thought arises, the body becomes like withered wood and the mind like extinguished ashes;
they take this to be the state of true and ultimate realization. Both of these approaches involve the use of a foolish and clumsy mind and are truly pitiable.

They are like pressing sand to extract oil or seeking milk from a horn of a rhinoceros; even if one were to pass through kalpas as numerous as dust motes, nothing at all would ever be gained. Furthermore, regarding the recognition of the nature of the mind:
Regarding that which acts as the self: who is it that knows the self? If the nature of the mind is the self, then who is it that knows the nature of the mind to be the self?
If both were the self, would there not then be two selves in one body? Reflect on this carefully.
Therefore, one knows that the nature of the mind is not the self. Furthermore, regarding those who take the non-arising of a single thought to be the ultimate reality:

if a single thought does not arise, how is this different from wood or stone? If being no different from wood or stone were the ultimate reality, then all wood and stone should be able to attain Buddhahood;
how could such a principle exist? Moreover, to be attached to the non-arising of a single thought—
To regard [anything] as "real" is itself attachment; attachment gives rise to conceptual thought—how could it be non-conceptual?
Furthermore, if you claim that not a single thought arises and yet you do not even cling to this as being real, then you are no different from an ignorant fool.
How, then, can you be called one who knows Chan and knows the Way? Reflect on this, reflect on it! Do not be negligent.
Mang asked: "What is the point of skillfully applying the mind? It means that as soon as a single thought arises, one asks, "What is my original face?
One simply observes who it is that gives rise to this thought. One must know that this one who gives rise to the thought is originally oneself giving rise to it;
how could it be another? Although it is oneself, there is no self to be found.
That which is without a self to be seen is the true self. Why? Because the self does not obtain a self, and because the self does not see a self.
It is like the eye not seeing itself, or a blade not cutting itself. Consider this: if the self were to obtain a self, there would be the error of two selves.
That is to say, if one identifies with and clings to this very momentary thought as being the self, one knows that the momentary thought is the self.
Furthermore, which one of these two is it? If both were the self, would that not result in there being two selves?
Moreover, if that which raises the thought is not the self, then one falls into nihilistic emptiness; this too is unacceptable.
Alternatively, if one seeks a self apart from this raising of the thought, it cannot be found throughout the bounds of the future. This principle is most difficult to understand clearly; one must...
Only through sincere and earnest devotion will there be a point of entry. If you can recognize that it is "I" who raises a thought, yet do not fall into the error of the view of permanence;
and if you can recognize that it is not "I" who raises a thought, yet do not incur the reproach of nihilistic emptiness—only then is this the skillful application of the mind. Be careful.
In the fourth chapter, a question was asked: "Is the original face existent? Is it non-existent? In response, he questioned him in turn:
"Is your present self existent? Is it non-existent? He replied: "My present self is existent. [The Master] asked:
He asked, "In the present, what do you take to be the self? He replied, "In the present, I take seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing to be the self.
He asked, "If in the present you take seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing to be the self, then who is it that knows seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing to be the self?
He replied, "The one who knows seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing is also the self."

[The Master replied: "It is so. [The opponent] objected: "If you say that seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing are you, and yet seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing are also you—if this were the case, would you not have two selves?

[The Master] asked: "If it follows from such a fault that my present self does not exist, then what do you take to be your present self? He then questioned him in return: "By what means do you establish your present existence?"
[The opponent asks: "Is it non-existent? [He] answers: "I see, hear, perceive, and know that it is non-existent. [The opponent] asks:
"Are you able to see, hear, perceive, and know in the present? [He] answers: "I am able to see, hear, perceive, and know. [The opponent] objects:
"Since you are able to see, hear, perceive, and know, how can it be non-existent? If you consider seeing, hearing, perceiving, and knowing to be the self, then..."

Furthermore, you still perceive a self and perceive seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing. It is like a gold ring that, once removed from the furnace and melted back into its original state as gold, no longer manifests the appearance of a ring.
If you perceive this seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing as being the self, [you are mistaken].

Then one will forever lose the true self’s abode. It is like gold that is fashioned back into a finger ring; once it has become a ring, the original nature of the gold is lost. Thus, an ancient verse says:
"If you know the delusion as delusion, then that very delusion is the truth. If you mistake the delusion for the truth, then even though it is the truth, it is still a delusion."
Reflect on this! Reflect on this! There is yet another verse: To know existence is difficult; non-existence is easy to find. To know non-existence is difficult; existence is easy to find.
When one clings to neither existence nor non-existence, One utters the lion’s roar of the Dharma.
In the fifth chapter, a question is asked: "Is the original face existent? Is it non-existent? The answer is: "It is neither existent nor non-existent. The questioner asks:
"How is it that it is neither existent nor non-existent? The answer is: "If the original face were existent..."
"Who is this original face? He replied, "It is my original face. He asked, "Who are you? He replied, "I am myself. He asked, "Who is the original face?
He replied, "It is also myself. [The opponent] raised an objection: "You are yourself; yet the original face is also..."
"You yourself—do you then have two selves? Therefore, the original face is not existence. Question:
"How then is it not non-existence? Answer: "If there is awareness, cognition, seeing, and hearing, these are still not the original face;
how much less so when there is no awareness, no cognition, no seeing, and no hearing—these are but false fabrications."
Is cessation its original face? Therefore, the original face is not non-existent. A question is asked:
"Ultimately, what is the original face? The answer is: "Just as the eye cannot see itself, it cannot be said to exist;
yet because the eye truly exists, it cannot be said to be non-existent. The original face is likewise."
It is likewise so. Because one cannot see it for oneself, it cannot be said to exist.
Because the original face truly exists from the beginning, it cannot be said to be non-existent. Contemplate this; contemplate this.
On the sixth day of the retreat, while he was sitting in meditation, a layman suddenly pushed open the door and entered. He asked, "Who are you? He replied, "My name is Wukong.
I have come specifically with a matter to seek your instruction. [The Master] said, "I have long heard it said that the Great Master knows 'that which is' (zhiyou)."
Yet one does not fall into the view of eternalism. One knows that things are non-existent, yet does not fall into the nihilistic emptiness of annihilation.

What is the meaning of "knowing non-existence without falling into the emptiness of annihilation"? The answer is: I now ask you; answer according to your own understanding. Do you now see forms with your eyes?
[The Master] asked: "Do you see? [The Disciple] replied: "I see. [The Master] asked: "Is your mind attached to form (*rūpa*)? [The Disciple] replied: "It is not attached.

"In the same way, when the ear hears sounds, the nose smells fragrances, the tongue tastes flavors, the body perceives tangibles, and the mind cognizes phenomena (*dharma*), does your mind become attached to these sounds, fragrances, flavors, tangibles, and phenomena?
[The Disciple] replied: "It is not attached. [The Master] asked: "At this point, what understanding remains within your mind? [The Disciple] replied: "At this point—"
At that time, within my mind there was no attachment whatsoever; only the "view of nothingness" remained. [The teacher] said:
"Even this view of nothingness must be cast away. He replied: "If even this view of nothingness is to be discarded, then within my mind there is nothing at all to be attained."
"Would this not fall into the emptiness of annihilation? He called out to him, "Wu-k'ung. The other replied, "Yes. [The Master] said, "Is it indeed the emptiness of annihilation?
He then exclaimed, "Excellent! I have greatly benefited from your instruction. Today I finally understand the meaning of realizing emptiness without falling into the view of nihilism.
How joyful this is! After bowing repeatedly in thanks, he departed.
The seventh chapter asks:
"Can the original face be seen? The answer is: "It cannot be seen. The question asks:
"Why can it not be seen? The answer is: "The original face is your very self; yet you wish to see your own self."
The original face. Are these not two original faces? For this reason, the original face cannot be seen.
Reflect upon this. He asked: "What is my own self? He replied:
"Is the one who is questioning right now not your own self? He asked, "May I take this questioner to be my own self?

He replied, "No. He asked, "Why may it not be so? He replied, "Although the questioner is indeed yourself, if you grasp at him as 'self,' then two selves will be created. That is to say, the questioner is you, and [the grasping subject] is you."
Furthermore, if you identify the questioner as yourself, would that not result in two selves? Reflect upon this.
The eighth question asks:
"Regarding the original face, how should one apply the mind to investigate it? The answer is: "One must not become attached to the six external sense objects."
The six internal faculties and the six consciousnesses—these are the points where the mind is correctly applied.

Question: If this is so, then there is no place for the mind to be applied; how, then, should one apply the mind? Answer: To have no place for the mind to be applied is precisely the point where the mind is correctly applied.

Any application of the mind to a specific place is invariably an attachment to signs (*nimitta*). Question: If there is no place for the mind to be applied, does this not result in falling into emptiness (*śūnyatā*)? Answer: [To be continued...]
[The Master] said: "Who is it that knows this falling into emptiness? [The monk] said: "It is I. [The Master] said: "Since this is you, how can you fall into emptiness? The monk asked:
"Is it permissible to take this very one who knows the falling into emptiness as the self? The Master replied: "It is not permissible. The monk asked: "Why is it not permissible? The Master replied:
"Though gold dust is precious, if it falls into the eye, it becomes a cataract."

These eight points above are all intended to refute the false attachments to the two extremes of annihilationism and eternalism, and to directly reveal the true meaning of the Middle Way and the Dharmakāya. Readers should examine them with careful attention.
Newly carved on the full moon day of the fourth month in the fifty-second year of the Qianlong era.
The printing blocks were preserved in the Chan Hall of Tiantong Temple in Changzhou Prefecture.
On the eighth day of the fourth month in the nineteenth year of the Guangxu era, they were re-carved by the student Ciqi of Taibai Peak in Ning and Yinzhou.
This manuscript contains many errors and corruptions;
I humbly entreat those with clear vision and vast compassion to correct it and circulate it—this is my earnest prayer.
Written at the Prajñā Hall of Tiantong Hongfa Chan Temple in the New Tripitaka Repository.
Even if one were to carry [the Buddha] upon one's head for kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, or offer one’s own body as a seat throughout the three thousandfold world system,
yet if one does not transmit the Dharma to deliver sentient beings, there would ultimately be no way to repay his kindness.
Only by upholding and maintaining the treasury of the True Dharma, proclaiming its teachings and principles to bestow them upon all living beings can one truly repay his grace.
Cultivating a single thought in accord with True Suchness is itself the true recompense for the Tathāgata.
